what: Color Palette from Image finds the main colours in a picture. It looks at every part of the picture, groups similar colours, and shows each one with its HEX, RGB and HSL code and how much of the picture it covers.
You choose from 2 to 16 colours and sort them by how much they are used, from dark to light, or in rainbow order. Tap anywhere on the picture to pick the exact colour of one spot.
Copy single codes, all HEX codes or CSS variables, or download a palette PNG to share. The picture never leaves your device.
uses: Get the exact colours from a logo for a website, slides or documents.
Build a colour scheme from a favourite photo or painting.
Find colours for text and buttons that match a header photo.
Pull the colours from a room or outfit photo.
Find paint or yarn colours from a reference picture.
Copy colours straight into CSS as variables.
tutorial: Click "Click or drop an image here" and choose a photo, logo or screenshot.
Move "Number of colours" from 2 to 16. The palette updates straight away.
"Most used first" shows the biggest areas first; "Dark to light" and "Rainbow order" help when building a scheme.
Each colour has "Copy HEX" and "Copy RGB". The bar above shows the colours in proportion.
Tap the picture to read the exact colour under your finger, then press "Copy".
Press "Download palette PNG", "Copy all HEX" or "Copy as CSS".
features: Choose how detailed the palette is.
Every colour in three formats, with its share of the picture.
Near-identical shades are joined so the palette stays useful.
Tap anywhere for the exact colour of one spot.
Get :root variables ready for your stylesheet.
Download a neat swatch card with the codes.

example.title: Worked example: website colours from a photo
example.text: Ken wants his café website to match a photo of the counter. He opens the photo, sets "Number of colours" to 6 and keeps "Most used first". The top colours are a warm brown #BA6837, a dark espresso #280A04 and a cream #EED5BD. He presses "Copy as CSS" and pastes --color-1 to --color-6 into his stylesheet, then downloads the palette PNG to send to his designer.

tips: Use fewer colours (4 to 6) for a clean scheme, more (10 to 16) to see the full range.
Crop the picture first if you only want the colours of one object.
For logos, pick the exact colour with a tap: averages can be slightly off at edges.
Check text contrast: dark colours from the palette usually make the best text colours.
